# Diagnosing Cold Weather Starting Issues on Small Engines

When a Kohler Courage 20 refuses to turn over in sub-40Â°F weather but runs perfectly once warm, the symptoms point toward combustion dynamics rather than mechanical failure. The fact that you get a strong blue spark and the starter motor spins freely rules out ignition coil failure or a seized flywheel. However, the behavior you describeâspinning until gas smellsâis a classic sign of flooding caused by an overly rich air-fuel mixture during the cold start sequence.

The core issue lies in how the carburetor manages the transition from choke to idle. In small engines like the one on your Troy Bilt Bronco, the choke plate physically blocks airflow to enrich the mixture for vaporizing fuel in cold conditions. If the linkage is loose or worn, the plate may not seat fully against the carburetor body. This creates a leak path that bypasses the restriction entirely, starving the engine of the extra fuel needed to ignite when temperatures drop.

Since you already replaced the carb gasket earlier this year, internal wear on the main jet or float is less likely, but mechanical linkage issues are common in older units. Before diving into complex disassembly, inspect the choke cable tension. You need to ensure that when you pull the handle, the plate hits a hard stop against the seat. If there is any slack where the spring pulls the plate back prematurely, cold starts will fail repeatedly. Adjusting this linkage often solves the issue without needing new parts.

Regarding the fuel age, three months is borderline acceptable for ethanol-blended gasoline in small engines, but oxidation can degrade performance. Ethanol absorbs moisture from the air over time, leading to phase separation where water settles at the bottom of the tank. If your gas sat in the tank during winter, condensation could have formed regardless of temperature. Draining the old fuel and filling with fresh gas is a low-cost diagnostic step that eliminates variables related to fuel quality.

The battery voltage reading of 13.4V indicates a healthy charge, and since the starter is only a year old, electrical power delivery is likely sufficient. Jumping the battery provided moderate success because it increased available current slightly, but flooding can occur even with ample cranking speed if the mixture is too rich. The smell of gas confirms that the engine is ingesting more fuel than the cold cylinder can vaporize, effectively drowning the spark plug in liquid hydrocarbons rather than allowing them to ignite.

Using starter fluid is a temporary workaround that bypasses the carburetor's inability to enrich the mix correctly. While your father-in-law warned against it, occasional use during extreme cold won't damage the engine if done sparingly. The real fix is restoring proper choke function or cleaning the idle circuit jets to ensure the transition to running on main fuel happens quickly once warmed up.

If adjusting the linkage does not resolve the issue, removing the carburetor for a bench test is the next logical step. You can verify that the choke plate seats fully and inspect the float level and needle valve adjustment. These are standard maintenance tasks that address the root cause of cold weather starting problems in air-cooled engines.
